S02.text: Students already enrolled and borrowing before July twenty twenty-six keep Grad PLUS for up to three more academic years, or for the time left in their program if that is shorter. New students like Leah still have the basic federal loan, a Direct Unsubsidized loan, up to twenty thousand five hundred dollars a year and one hundred thousand dollars total, with higher limits in professional programs like medicine or law. When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

takes.asr: Students already enrolled and borrowing before July 2026 keep grad plus for up to three more academic years or for the time left in their program if that is shorter. New students like Leah still have the basic federal loan, a direct unsubsidized loan up to $20 ,500 a year and $100 ,000 total with higher limits in professional programs like medicine or law. When a program costs more than that after other aid, the rest can come from a private lender, and that's where Leah's two offers come from. Same lender, same amount, two kinds of rate.

S03.text: Both are for fifty thousand dollars over ten years, illustrative numbers, not a real lender's offer. The variable loan's first payment is five hundred ninety-three dollars and fifty-one cents, about forty dollars less a month than the fixed six hundred thirty-three dollars and thirty-eight cents. A fixed rate never changes, so neither does the payment. A variable rate follows a market interest rate, so the rate and the payment rise and fall with it, and nobody knows where it goes next. The distance between the two starting rates is what this video calls the head start. Leah's fixed rate is nine percent and her variable rate starts at seven point five percent, so her head start is one point five points. A point here means one percentage point of interest. Real offers differ: a head start can be bigger, smaller, zero, or negative, with the variable rate starting higher.

S04.text: This video replays Leah's illustrative loan through every ten-year stretch of U.S. interest rates since January nineteen fifty-four. "Worth it" gets one plain meaning here: how often the variable loan cost more in total interest than the nine percent fixed loan, and how much more at worst. Then the replay moves the head start, from a variable rate three points under the fixed rate to one one point over it, to see where that history changes. By the end there's a line that any real offer can be held up against, including yours. This is history, not a forecast.

S05.text: [curious] And the first result looks like a contradiction. Leah's variable rate rose above nine percent at some point in about three in four stretches. Yet it cost more in total interest in about one in seven. That's more than one in four for starts from nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty and about one in thirty from nineteen eighty-one on, and the worst stretch cost eleven thousand two hundred nineteen dollars more. The reason both are true is the head start.

S06.text: Every month the variable rate sits below nine percent, Leah pays less interest than on the fixed loan, and that saving builds a cushion. The cushion grows fastest at the start, when she owes the most, so every point of rate is charged on the biggest balance. When the rate later climbs above nine percent, the extra interest has to use up that cushion before the variable loan has cost more overall. A short jump above nine percent only dents it; emptying it needs rates that rise early and stay high for years. In a stretch where rates drift down, the cushion just keeps growing.

S07.text: Here's how the replay works. A real variable rate is the lender's own index plus a fixed margin, and the replay needs a much longer record than that index has. So it uses a stand-in with a long U.S. record, the rate on three-month Treasury bills, and sets the margin so that Leah's rate starts at seven point five percent. From then on, her rate rises and falls exactly as much as the Treasury bill rate did. The first replay starts in January nineteen fifty-four and runs for ten years, and the next starts one month later, and so on, up to September twenty sixteen. Each one is set against the nine percent fixed loan over the same ten years. Neighbouring stretches share most of their years, so they are not independent tries, and the data is U.S. only.

S08.text: And the two halves of the record are very different. From nineteen fifty-four to nineteen eighty, the Treasury bill rate mostly climbed, in waves. It peaked at sixteen point three percent in May nineteen eighty-one, then mostly drifted down over the following decades, with big swings. Same loan, same head start; the only difference is where in history it began. Loans started in the climbing years often met rates that rose early and stayed high, and loans started after the peak mostly rode rates down. The best stretch began in August nineteen eighty-one, near that peak, and cost fifteen thousand two hundred ninety-five dollars less than the fixed loan. But across the nineteen fifty-four-to-nineteen eighty starts more than one in four cost more, against about one in thirty from nineteen eighty-one on, and the worst, from April nineteen seventy-seven, cost eleven thousand two hundred nineteen dollars more.
